title: TED drive pack
description: 33 TED talks for a long drive: leadership, communication, mindset, happiness, ideas, Indian speakers

items.title: 01 · Simon Sinek: How great leaders inspire action
items.notes:
**Big idea:** People follow leaders and buy from companies because of why they do things, not what they do.

**Key points:**
- The Golden Circle has three rings: Why, How, What. Most firms talk from the outside in. Inspiring ones start with Why.
- Apple opens with its belief in challenging the status quo. Dell and Gateway had the same talent but failed outside their core.
- The limbic brain drives trust and decisions but has no language. That is why a choice can just not feel right.
- The Wright brothers had no funding or degrees but a cause. Langley had $50,000 and the press, and quit the day they flew.
- Change spreads past 15 to 18% adoption only after early adopters buy into the belief. Martin Luther King said I have a dream, not I have a plan.

**Remember:** "People don’t buy what you do; they buy why you do it."

**Use it at work:**
- Open roadmaps, reorgs and promotion pitches with the purpose first, then the approach, then the deliverables.
- In interviews, ask candidates why they do their work, and hire people who believe what your team believes.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/great-leaders-inspire-action-simon-sinek-transcript/

items.title: 02 · Simon Sinek: Why good leaders make you feel safe
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Good leaders build a circle of safety, so people trust each other and face outside threats together.

**Key points:**
- Captain William Swenson ran into fire in Afghanistan to save his men. Heroes say they would have done it for me.
- Trust and cooperation are feelings. A leader cannot order them, but can create the setting for them.
- A gate agent scolded a passenger because she feared losing her job. Fear of leaders, not poor hiring, caused it.
- In 2008 Barry-Wehmiller lost 30% of orders. Bob Chapman chose a four-week unpaid furlough for all, not layoffs, and saved $20 million.
- In the Marines, officers eat last. Leaders take the risk first so their people can be safe.

**Remember:** "Leadership is a choice. It is not a rank."

**Use it at work:**
- When cuts or deadlines hit, protect your people first and share the pain visibly, starting with yourself.
- In 1:1s, check whether people fear you or fear breaking rules, and remove that fear so they speak up early.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/why-good-leaders-make-you-feel-safe-simon-sinek-transcript/

items.title: 03 · Roselinde Torres: What it takes to be a great leader
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Great 21st-century leaders look ahead, build diverse networks, and have the courage to drop what made them successful.

**Key points:**
- A study of 4,000 companies found 58% had big talent gaps in critical leadership roles, despite training and coaching.
- Torres spent 25 years watching leaders and advised over 200 CEOs. She studied Nelson Mandela and presidential libraries.
- Question one: where are you looking to see the next change? Your calendar, reading and travel show the answer.
- Question two: how diverse is your network? Different people help you spot patterns and find new answers.
- Question three: are you willing to abandon a past practice? This takes the stamina to hear your idea called naive.

**Remember:** "Great leaders dare to be different."

**Use it at work:**
- Audit your calendar each month. Add time with people outside engineering, such as sellers, ops and customers.
- In 1:1s with senior engineers, ask which habit that made them successful they should now drop, and do the same yourself.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/what-it-takes-to-be-a-great-leader-roselinde-torres-transcript/

items.title: 04 · Stanley McChrystal: Listen, learn ... then lead
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Leading a spread-out, younger and more expert team means you listen and learn first, then lead.

**Key points:**
- After 9/11, McChrystal's force spread across more than 20 countries. He led by video calls, chat, email and phone.
- After a failed mission, he had to rebuild trust without being able to put a hand on a shoulder.
- A wounded Ranger sergeant told him he was in sixth grade on 9/11. The generation gap was real.
- Junior soldiers knew the new tech and tactics best. He had to be transparent and accept reverse mentoring.
- As a young officer he failed a training exercise badly. His battalion commander told him he did great anyway.

**Remember:** "leaders can let you fail and yet not let you be a failure."

**Use it at work:**
- Set up reverse mentoring with junior engineers on new tools like AI coding agents, and say openly what you are learning.
- When someone on your team fails, treat the failure as data in the 1:1, and make clear you still back them.

Source transcript: https://digitalcast.jp/v/11625/

items.title: 05 · Margaret Heffernan: Forget the pecking order at work
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Teams win through social connection and helpfulness, not by collecting superstar individuals.

**Key points:**
- William Muir at Purdue bred a superflock of top egg-laying hens. After six generations only three survived. They pecked the rest to death.
- An MIT study found the best groups were not the highest IQ. They had social sensitivity, equal speaking time and more women.
- At Arup, an engineer asked for help on horse waste for the Beijing equestrian center and solved it in under a day.
- Social capital is trust that builds over time. Shared coffee breaks at one firm were linked to $15 million more profit.
- On the CFC phase-out, Frank Maslen's team ran with no stars and one standard: the best imaginable.

**Remember:** "Companies don't have ideas; only people do."

**Use it at work:**
- Reward helping others in reviews and promotion cases, not just individual output, and watch for star players who suppress peers.
- Make sure every voice gets airtime in design reviews and standups, and create time for the team to know each other.

Source transcript: https://cs.brown.edu/courses/cs180/sources/2015_TED_Talk_TeamManagement_Heffernan.pdf

items.title: 06 · Amy Edmondson: Building a psychologically safe workplace
items.notes:
**Big idea:** People stay silent at work to protect their image, and leaders must build psychological safety so they speak up.

**Key points:**
- Three silent moments: a nurse who does not query a dose, a trainee pilot who lets a mistake pass, an executive who hides doubts on a takeover.
- People avoid looking ignorant, incompetent, intrusive or negative. So they do not ask, admit, offer ideas or critique.
- In her hospital study, better teams seemed to make more errors. In fact they were more willing to report and discuss them.
- Three leader moves: frame work as a learning problem, admit your own fallibility, and model curiosity with lots of questions.
- Safety and accountability are separate. High on both is the learning zone. High accountability alone is the anxiety zone.

**Remember:** "Maybe the better teams aren’t making more mistakes, maybe they’re more willing to discuss them."

**Use it at work:**
- Start incident reviews and planning by naming the uncertainty and saying you may miss things you need to hear.
- Keep high standards, but thank people who raise bad news early, so the team lands in the learning zone, not the anxiety zone.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/building-a-psychologically-safe-workplace-amy-edmondson-transcript/

items.title: 07 · Tim Harford: Trial, error and the God complex
items.notes:
**Big idea:** The world is too complex for any expert to get right first time, so we should solve problems by trial and error.

**Key points:**
- The God complex is the belief that you are right whatever the complexity. Harford sees it in economists, business leaders and politicians.
- Unilever could not design a detergent nozzle by maths. It made 10 random variants, kept the best, and repeated for 45 generations.
- Archie Cochrane tested home versus hospital care after heart attacks. When he showed the results, hospitals were the riskier option.
- Twyla Tharp turned bad reviews of Moving Out into a fix list. The show ran for years and won two Tony Awards.
- We hate to admit losses, so we stay on failing paths. Schools teach that each problem has one right answer.

**Remember:** "Until then, I'm going to keep banging on about trial and error and why we should abandon the God complex."

**Use it at work:**
- Run small, cheap experiments such as A/B tests and spikes before big design bets, and kill losers fast.
- Turn harsh feedback on a launch or a talk into a checklist and fix items one by one, like Tharp did.

Source transcript: https://www.npr.org/transcripts/487609615

items.title: 08 · Dan Pink: The puzzle of motivation
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Rewards help with simple tasks but hurt creative work, which runs best on autonomy, mastery and purpose.

**Key points:**
- In Sam Glucksberg's candle problem test, people offered cash took about 3.5 minutes longer to solve it.
- When the task was made simple, the cash group did better. Rewards narrow focus, which only helps with clear tasks.
- In Dan Ariely's MIT study, bigger rewards led to worse results in 8 of 9 tasks. A test in Madurai, India, found the same.
- Atlassian's FedEx Days and Google's 20% time give engineers freedom. Gmail and Google News came out of it.
- Results Only Work Environments drop fixed schedules. Productivity and engagement rise and turnover falls.

**Remember:** "This is one of the most robust findings in social science, and also one of the most ignored."

**Use it at work:**
- Give engineers real autonomy over how they solve a problem, and run hack days with a demo the next morning.
- In 1:1s, talk about mastery and purpose, such as skills to grow and customer impact, not just ratings and bonuses.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/transcript-dan-pink-discusses-the-puzzle-of-motivation-at-ted-talk-conference/

items.title: 09 · Adam Grant: Are you a giver or a taker?
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Givers sit at both the bottom and the top of success, and culture depends most on keeping takers out.

**Key points:**
- People act as givers, takers or matchers. In surveys of over 30,000 people, most are matchers.
- Generous engineers did the least work and generous medical students got the lowest grades. Yet givers were also the top performers.
- Teams with more helping, sharing and mentoring had better profits, customer satisfaction and retention.
- One taker hurts a culture two to three times more than one giver helps. Agreeableness does not tell you who is who.
- Adam Rifkin uses the five-minute favor. Asking for help matters too: 75 to 90% of giving starts with a request.

**Remember:** "Givers are overrepresented at the bottom and at the top of every success metric that I can track."

**Use it at work:**
- In interviews, ask for four people whose careers the candidate helped. Takers name the powerful, givers name people below them.
- Protect your givers from burnout by setting limits, and make it normal on the team to ask for help.

Source transcript: https://digitalcast.jp/v/25424/

items.title: 10 · Julian Treasure: How to speak so that people want to listen
items.notes:
**Big idea:** People listen to you when your words are honest and kind and your voice is used with skill.

**Key points:**
- Seven deadly sins of speaking: gossip, judging, negativity, complaining, excuses, exaggeration, and dogmatism.
- HAIL is the base of powerful speech: Honesty, Authenticity, Integrity and Love.
- The vocal toolbox has register, timbre, prosody, pace, pitch and volume. A lower chest voice sounds more weighty.
- Use silence instead of filler words. Avoid a monotone, and avoid ending every statement like a question.
- Warm up before big talks: deep sighs, lip trills, la sounds and a siren from high to low.

**Remember:** "complaining is viral misery. It’s not spreading sunshine and lightness in the world."

**Use it at work:**
- Before leadership reviews or all-hands, warm up your voice, slow down, and pause in place of saying um.
- Model HAIL in 1:1s and retros, and stop gossip and complaining about other teams when you hear it.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/how-to-speak-so-that-people-want-to-listen-by-julian-treasure-transcript/

items.title: 11 · Julian Treasure: 5 ways to listen better
items.notes:
**Big idea:** We are losing the skill of listening, and five simple habits can help us listen with intent again.

**Key points:**
- We spend about 60% of our talk time listening, but we keep only about 25% of what we hear.
- Listening is making meaning from sound. Filters such as culture, mood and intention shape what we notice.
- Recordings, noise, headphones and shouting headlines all wear down our listening.
- Exercises: three minutes of silence a day, the mixer (pick out sound channels), and savouring everyday sounds.
- Change your listening position on purpose, and use RASA: Receive, Appreciate, Summarise, Ask.

**Remember:** "We retain just 25 percent of what we hear."

**Use it at work:**
- Use RASA in 1:1s: give full attention, nod and say OK, sum up starting with so, then ask questions.
- Before a tough meeting or interview, pick your listening position on purpose, such as critical, empathetic or curious.

Source transcript: https://www.dailygood.org/story/1844/julian-treasure-on-5-ways-to-listen-better-julian-treasure/

items.title: 12 · Celeste Headlee: 10 ways to have a better conversation
items.notes:
**Big idea:** A good conversation comes down to one thing: be genuinely interested in the other person.

**Key points:**
- A Pew study of 10,000 US adults found Americans more polarized than at any time in recorded history.
- Common tips like eye contact and nodding are useless; if you are really paying attention, you do not need to fake it.
- Her rules include: don't multitask, don't pontificate, ask open-ended questions, say when you don't know, and stay out of the weeds.
- Don't equate your experience with theirs; the moment is not about you.
- Listening matters most: we speak about 225 words a minute but can listen at up to 500, so the mind wanders.

**Remember:** "Everybody is an expert in something."

**Use it at work:**
- In 1:1s, put the laptop away, ask "What was that like?" instead of yes/no questions, and resist jumping to your own story.
- In interviews, enter assuming the candidate knows something you don't; keep your own talking short.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/celeste-headlee-on-10-ways-to-have-a-better-conversation-full-transcript/

items.title: 13 · Susan Cain: The power of introverts
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Introverts do their best work in quiet, and workplaces and schools that prize constant group work waste their talent.

**Key points:**
- A third to a half of people are introverts. Introversion is about response to stimulation; shyness is fear of social judgment.
- Adam Grant at Wharton found introverted leaders often get better results with proactive employees, because they let them run with ideas.
- Darwin walked alone, Dr. Seuss worked in a bell-tower office, and Wozniak designed the first Apple computer alone at HP.
- Groups follow the most dominant talker, yet being the best talker has zero correlation with having the best ideas.
- Her three asks: stop the madness of constant group work, go to the wilderness, and open your suitcase and share what is inside.

**Remember:** "Shyness is about fear of social judgment."

**Use it at work:**
- Send agendas early and allow written input, so quiet engineers can contribute before the loudest voice sets the direction.
- Protect focus time and do not read quietness in a 1:1 or interview as low ability or low leadership potential.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/quiet-power-introverts-susan-cain-transcript/

items.title: 14 · Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie: The danger of a single story
items.notes:
**Big idea:** When we know only one story about a person or a place, we flatten them into a stereotype and strip away their dignity.

**Key points:**
- As a child in Nigeria she wrote about white characters who played in snow and ate apples, because those were the only books she read.
- She pitied Fide's poor family until she saw a beautiful basket his brother had made.
- Her American roommate was surprised she spoke English well and asked to hear her "tribal music."
- A professor said her novel was not authentically African because the characters were middle-class and educated.
- In Guadalajara she felt ashamed that she had absorbed the single story of Mexicans as immigrants.

**Remember:** "Stories matter. Many stories matter."

**Use it at work:**
- Before judging an engineer on one bad incident or one review comment, collect more data points and more voices.
- In hiring and calibration, notice when a candidate or team is being reduced to a single label, and ask for the rest of the story.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/danger-single-story-chimamanda-adichie-transcript/

items.title: 15 · Carol Dweck: The power of believing that you can improve
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Believing that ability can grow, the power of "yet", changes how people react to difficulty and failure.

**Key points:**
- A Chicago high school gave the grade "Not Yet" instead of a fail, so students saw themselves on a learning curve.
- Given problems slightly too hard, some 10-year-olds loved the challenge; fixed-mindset kids said they might cheat next time.
- Brain scans showed growth-mindset students engaging deeply with errors, while fixed-mindset students barely processed them.
- Praise process, effort, strategy and progress, not talent; a University of Washington math game that rewarded process raised effort and persistence.
- In one year a South Bronx fourth-grade class rose to number one in New York State on the math test.

**Remember:** "Instead of luxuriating in the power of yet, they were gripped in the tyranny of now."

**Use it at work:**
- In feedback and 1:1s, praise the approach and the learning, not "you're so smart"; frame gaps as "not yet."
- In interviews, give a harder follow-up and watch how the candidate handles struggle, not just whether they reach the answer.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/the-power-of-believing-that-you-can-improve-by-carol-dweck-transcript/

items.title: 16 · Angela Lee Duckworth: Grit: The power of passion and perseverance
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Grit, meaning passion and perseverance for long-term goals, predicts success better than talent or IQ.

**Key points:**
- At 27 she left management consulting to teach seventh-grade math in New York and saw that IQ did not separate her best and worst students.
- She studied West Point cadets, National Spelling Bee contestants, rookie teachers in tough schools and salespeople; grit predicted who succeeded.
- In Chicago public schools, grittier juniors were more likely to graduate, even after matching on family income, test scores and safety.
- Talent does not make you gritty; in her data grit is unrelated or even inversely related to talent.
- She admits science does not yet know how to build grit; Carol Dweck's growth mindset is the best idea she has heard.

**Remember:** "Grit is living life like it's a marathon, not a sprint."

**Use it at work:**
- In hiring, probe for sustained effort on long, hard projects, not only raw brilliance in a short puzzle.
- Set long-horizon goals with your team and celebrate persistence through setbacks, not just quick wins.

Source transcript: https://tea4avcastro.tea.state.tx.us/thl/G8ELAR.W2.L1.grit-the-power-of-passion-and-perseverance.pdf

items.title: 17 · Kathryn Schulz: On being wrong
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Being wrong feels exactly like being right, so we should hold our certainty loosely and treat error as human, not shameful.

**Key points:**
- Error blindness: like the cartoon coyote running off a cliff, we feel nothing until we look down.
- At Beth Israel Deaconess in Boston, a surgeon operated on the wrong leg because he felt he was on the correct side.
- When people disagree with us, we assume they are ignorant, then idiots, then deliberately lying.
- We learn as children that people who get things wrong are lazy or foolish, so we become perfectionists.
- St. Augustine wrote "I err therefore I am" long before Descartes; our capacity for error comes from imagining the world as it isn't.

**Remember:** "It does feel like something to be wrong; it feels like being right."

**Use it at work:**
- In design reviews and incident postmortems, ask "what would make us wrong here?" and make blameless analysis the norm.
- Model it yourself: say "maybe I'm wrong" in front of the team so others can admit mistakes early.

Source transcript: https://digitalcast.jp/v/11603/

items.title: 18 · Matt Cutts: Try something new for 30 days
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Trying something new for 30 days is a simple, low-risk way to build habits and change your life.

**Key points:**
- Feeling stuck in a rut, he borrowed the 30-day challenge idea from Morgan Spurlock.
- Thirty days is about the right time to add a new habit or drop an old one, like watching the news.
- The months became more memorable; he could recall where he was and what he was doing.
- Harder challenges built confidence: from desk-bound programmer to biking to work, and later hiking Mt. Kilimanjaro.
- He wrote a 50,000-word novel in a month by writing 1,667 words a day; small, sustainable changes tend to stick better than big crazy ones.

**Remember:** "What are you waiting for?"

**Use it at work:**
- Run 30-day experiments with the team, such as a new standup format or a code review rule, then keep or drop it.
- For your own growth, pick one leadership habit, like a weekly skip-level chat, and commit to it for 30 days.

Source transcript: https://www.palmbeachstate.edu/academicaffairs/Documents/ENC1101DiagnosticTedTalk.pdf

items.title: 19 · Andy Puddicombe: All it takes is 10 mindful minutes
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Ten minutes a day of stepping back from your thoughts can bring more calm, focus and clarity to your whole life.

**Key points:**
- He asks when you last spent 10 minutes doing nothing at all; we care for cars, clothes and hair more than the mind.
- At about 20, overwhelmed by difficult events, he left his degree and went to the Himalayas to train as a monk.
- He cites research that our minds are lost in thought 47% of the time, and that this makes us less happy.
- Meditation is not stopping thoughts; it is watching them come and go without judgment, with a relaxed yet focused mind.
- His juggling demo: focus too hard and you tense up, relax too much and you drop the balls.

**Remember:** "We can't change every little thing that happens to us in life, but we can change the way that we experience it."

**Use it at work:**
- Take 10 quiet minutes before high-stakes 1:1s, reviews or presentations, so you respond instead of react.
- During incidents, notice the anxiety spiral of worrying about worrying, and bring the team back to the next concrete step.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/all-it-takes-is-10-mindful-minutes-by-andy-puddicombe-full-transcript/

items.title: 20 · Tim Urban: Inside the mind of a master procrastinator
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Procrastination is a fight between your rational self and an Instant Gratification Monkey, and the worst kind hides where there are no deadlines.

**Key points:**
- He wrote his 90-page senior thesis in the last 72 hours, with two all-nighters.
- The Monkey lives only in the present and steers you into the Dark Playground, where leisure is soaked in guilt and dread.
- The Panic Monster wakes when a deadline nears and scares the Monkey away; his TED talk only started once his face was on the website.
- Long-term goals with no deadline, like a career change, exercise or family time, never wake the Panic Monster.
- His Life Calendar shows a 90-year life as a grid of about 4,680 weeks.

**Remember:** "We need to stay aware of the Instant Gratification Monkey."

**Use it at work:**
- Give long, important work, like tech debt or career growth plans, real milestones and check-ins, so it does not drift.
- In 1:1s, ask each report what important thing has no deadline, and help them set one.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/inside-the-mind-of-a-master-procrastinator-by-tim-urban-full-transcript/

items.title: 21 · Robert Waldinger: What makes a good life? Lessons from the longest study on happiness
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Good, close relationships, not wealth, fame or working harder, keep us happier and healthier as we age.

**Key points:**
- The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed 724 men for 75 years, since 1938: Harvard sophomores and boys from poor Boston neighborhoods.
- Socially connected people were happier, healthier and lived longer; loneliness was toxic, and over one in five Americans report being lonely.
- Quality beats quantity: high-conflict marriages with little affection were very bad for health.
- At 50, cholesterol did not predict health at 80; relationship satisfaction did.
- Men who could count on their partners had sharper memories in their 80s, even if they bickered.

**Remember:** "Good relationships keep us happier and healthier. Period."

**Use it at work:**
- Treat trust on the team as a real asset: invest in 1:1s, team rituals and people who can rely on each other in hard times.
- Remind yourself and your reports that nobody wishes on their deathbed for more office hours; protect time for family.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/robert-waldinger-on-the-good-life-at-tedxbeaconstreet-full-transcript/

items.title: 22 · Kelly McGonigal: How to make stress your friend
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Stress harms you mainly when you believe it is harmful; seeing it as helpful, and reaching out to others, changes how your body responds.

**Key points:**
- A study of 30,000 US adults over eight years: high stress raised the risk of dying by 43%, but only for those who believed stress was harmful.
- Researchers estimated 182,000 Americans died early over those eight years from that belief.
- In a Harvard social stress test, people taught to see a pounding heart as preparation felt more confident, and their blood vessels stayed relaxed.
- Stress releases oxytocin, which pushes us to seek and give support and helps protect the heart.
- In a study of about 1,000 adults, each major stressful event raised death risk by 30%, except in people who spent time helping others.

**Remember:** "Caring created resilience"

**Use it at work:**
- Before launches or big presentations, reframe the racing heart for yourself and the team as the body getting ready.
- During crunch periods, build in peer help and check-ins, so stress turns into connection instead of isolation.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/make-stress-friend-kelly-mcgonigal-transcript/

items.title: 23 · Shawn Achor: The happy secret to better work
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Happiness comes before success, not after it, because a positive brain works better.

**Key points:**
- Only 10% of long-term happiness is predicted by your external world; 90% by how your brain processes it.
- Only 25% of job success is predicted by IQ; 75% by optimism, social support and seeing stress as a challenge.
- A brain at positive is 31% more productive; salespeople are 37% better; doctors are 19% faster and more accurate.
- Dopamine from positivity turns on the brain's learning centers.
- Two minutes a day for 21 days rewires the brain: three new gratitudes, journaling one good moment, exercise, meditation, a random act of kindness.

**Remember:** "The absence of disease is not health." If success always comes first, happiness stays pushed over the horizon.

**Use it at work:**
- Open team meetings or 1:1s with one specific win from the last day before diving into problems.
- Try a 21-day team experiment: one thank-you message to a colleague each morning, and watch engagement.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/shawn-achor-happy-secret-better-work-transcript/

items.title: 24 · Dan Gilbert: The surprising science of happiness
items.notes:
**Big idea:** We can make our own happiness, so we overestimate how much any outcome will change how we feel.

**Key points:**
- A year later, lottery winners and paraplegics are about equally happy with their lives.
- Impact bias: we overrate how good or bad future events will feel.
- Synthetic happiness, made when we do not get what we wanted, is as real as natural happiness.
- Moreese Bickham, after 37 years in prison for a crime he did not commit, called it a glorious experience; Pete Best said he was happier than he would have been with the Beatles.
- Monet prints and photography studies: people grow to like what they own, but only when the choice is irreversible. Even amnesiacs liked the print they owned.

**Remember:** "Synthetic happiness is what we make when we don't get what we wanted." Our longings and worries are to some degree overblown.

**Use it at work:**
- When a promotion, project or role does not go someone's way, help them see they will adapt faster than they expect.
- Make decisions final once made; endless reversibility (re-opening reorgs or tool choices) lowers satisfaction.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/dan-gilbert-on-the-surprising-science-of-happiness-at-ted-full-transcript/

items.title: 25 · Daniel Kahneman: The riddle of experience vs. memory
items.notes:
**Big idea:** We have two selves, one that lives through moments and one that remembers them, and the remembering self makes our choices.

**Key points:**
- Colonoscopy study: the patient with longer, more total pain remembered it as better, because the ending was milder.
- A screech at the end of a symphony recording did not ruin the experience, only the memory of it.
- Vacation test: if all photos were destroyed and your memory erased, would you choose the same trip?
- The psychological present is about three seconds; most moments leave no trace.
- Gallup data on about 600,000 Americans: below $60,000 a year people are less happy day to day; above it, experienced happiness is flat, but life satisfaction keeps rising with income.

**Remember:** "We actually don't choose between experiences, we choose between memories of experiences."

**Use it at work:**
- Design endings on purpose: close hard sprints, launches and offsites on a high note, since that shapes how the team remembers them.
- In reviews and 1:1s, ask about day-to-day experience, not just the story; they can differ a lot.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/the-riddle-of-experience-vs-memory-daniel-kahneman-transcript/

items.title: 26 · Brené Brown: The power of vulnerability
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Connection needs vulnerability, and people who feel worthy of love and belonging are the ones who dare to be seen.

**Key points:**
- A one-year study became six years: thousands of stories, hundreds of long interviews, focus groups.
- Wholehearted people had the courage to be imperfect and fully embraced vulnerability.
- They believed what made them vulnerable made them beautiful.
- You cannot selectively numb emotion: numb pain and you also numb joy, gratitude and happiness.
- Her own findings led to what she calls a breakdown and a year of therapy fighting vulnerability.

**Remember:** "You're imperfect, and you're wired for struggle, but you are worthy of love and belonging."

**Use it at work:**
- Model it: say I don't know or I got this wrong in team meetings and retros, so others feel safe to do the same.
- In 1:1s, ask what is hard right now, and listen without fixing.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/power-vulnerability-brene-brown-transcript/

items.title: 27 · Ric Elias: 3 things I learned while my plane crashed
items.notes:
**Big idea:** A near-death moment on a crashing plane taught one man to live now, choose happiness over being right, and focus on being a good dad.

**Key points:**
- He sat in seat 1D on the plane that landed on the Hudson River after the engines went quiet.
- The pilot said three words: brace for impact.
- Lesson 1: it all changes in an instant, so stop postponing things; he no longer saves good wine for later.
- Lesson 2: he regretted time wasted on things that did not matter, so he cut negative energy and stopped trying to be right.
- Lesson 3: dying was not scary; his only wish was to see his kids grow up.

**Remember:** "I no longer try to be right. I choose to be happy."

**Use it at work:**
- In conflicts, ask whether winning the argument matters more than the relationship and the outcome.
- Do not defer the recognition, the hard conversation or the career talk to next quarter.

Source transcript: https://www.npr.org/transcripts/195233144

items.title: 28 · Ken Robinson: Do schools kill creativity?
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Creativity is as important as literacy, but schools teach it out of children by stigmatizing mistakes.

**Key points:**
- A girl drawing God tells her teacher people will know what God looks like in a minute; children take chances.
- In his son's nativity play, a boy improvised: Frank sent this.
- Every school system ranks maths and languages at the top, then humanities, with the arts at the bottom.
- Academic inflation: degrees are worth less, so the system keeps demanding more qualifications.
- Gillian Lynne, labelled as having a learning problem, was told by a doctor she was a dancer; she became a famous choreographer.

**Remember:** "If you're not prepared to be wrong, you'll never come up with anything original."

**Use it at work:**
- Make it safe to be wrong: reward experiments and blameless postmortems, not only correct answers.
- In hiring and reviews, look past narrow academic signals for talents people show when they are in their element.

Source transcript: https://sonix.ai/resources/full-transcript-do-schools-kill-creativity-sir-ken-robinson-ted/

items.title: 29 · Elizabeth Gilbert: Your elusive creative genius
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Instead of believing you are a genius, think of yourself as having one; it takes the crushing pressure off creative work.

**Key points:**
- After Eat, Pray, Love, people kept asking if she feared she could never top it.
- The Greeks had daemons and the Romans a genius: outside spirits that helped, so success and failure were not all on the artist.
- Poet Ruth Stone felt poems coming across the fields and had to run like hell to catch them.
- Tom Waits, hearing a melody while driving, told the sky he was busy driving.
- In North Africa, crowds chanted Allah at a transcendent dance; in Spain this became Olé.

**Remember:** "Don't be afraid. Don't be daunted. Just do your job." Keep showing up for your part, whatever the result.

**Use it at work:**
- After a big win or a flop, separate the person from the outcome; judge effort and craft, not just results.
- Coach high performers who freeze after success to keep shipping their part of the work.

Source transcript: https://www.alexanderjarvis.com/your-elusive-creative-genius-by-elizabeth-gilbert/

items.title: 30 · Devdutt Pattanaik: East vs. West: the myths that mystify
items.notes:
**Big idea:** Each culture runs on its own myths, and those myths shape how people do business and manage.

**Key points:**
- Alexander meets a gymnosophist: one is conquering the world, the other experiencing nothingness, and each thinks the other a fool.
- One life versus many lives: Western thought leans to binary logic, absolute truth and standardization; Indian thought to fuzzy, contextual thinking.
- Ganesha wins the race by circling his parents: You went around the world. I went around my world.
- The standard business model of vision, mission, values and processes mirrors a journey to one promised land; Indian thinking sees many promised lands.
- People who have done business in India often show exasperation, because the logic differs.

**Remember:** "My truth is my truth. Your truth is your truth." Within infinite myths lies the eternal truth.

**Use it at work:**
- When working with global teams or stakeholders, ask what their unspoken beliefs are before judging their process as wrong.
- In presentations, frame the same plan for both a fixed-goal and a context-driven audience.

Source transcript: https://digitalcast.jp/v/13662/

items.title: 31 · Shashi Tharoor: Why nations should pursue soft power
items.notes:
**Big idea:** In an information age, a country wins by telling a better story, not by military or economic might alone.

**Key points:**
- Joseph Nye's soft power: the ability to attract others through culture, political values and foreign policies.
- Bollywood carries Indian culture worldwide; he tells of a Senegalese woman watching Bollywood films without understanding the dialogue.
- Yoga, Ayurveda and Indian cuisine spread India's influence.
- Democracy and pluralism: you need agreement on the ground rules for disagreeing, not on everything.
- India has managed to maintain consensus on how to survive without consensus.

**Remember:** "It's the country that tells a better story that prevails." Governments aren't very good at telling stories.

**Use it at work:**
- Build your team's influence through reputation, open demos and helpful docs, not only through escalations.
- For a promotion or cross-team pitch, tell a clear story people want to join, not just a list of numbers.

Source transcript: https://singjupost.com/why-nations-should-pursue-soft-power-shashi-tharoor-transcript/

items.title: 32 · Nandan Nilekani: Ideas for India's future
items.notes:
**Big idea:** India's progress depends on ideas, which he sorts into four groups: ideas that have arrived, ideas in progress, ideas in battle, and ideas to anticipate.

**Key points:**
- Arrived: people seen as an asset, not a burden; a young country in an ageing world; English seen as opportunity; technology; deeper trust in democracy.
- In progress: growing consensus on primary education, infrastructure, cities as engines of growth, and India as one market.
- In battle: contested areas such as labour reform and overregulated higher education.
- To anticipate: future problems like lifestyle diseases, energy and the environment, so India can avoid rich countries' mistakes.
- The demographic dividend pays off only with investment in education, health and jobs.

**Remember:** Transcript not available, so paraphrased: a society moves when ideas reach consensus, so watch which ideas are still being fought over.

**Use it at work:**
- Map your team's initiatives the same way: settled, in progress, contested, and next-year bets.
- Spend leadership time where alignment is missing, not on ideas that are already settled.

items.title: 33 · Arunachalam Muruganantham: How I started a sanitary napkin revolution!
items.notes:
**Big idea:** A school dropout from Coimbatore, moved by his wife's struggle, built a simple low-cost machine so rural women could make and sell their own sanitary pads.

**Key points:**
- He saw his wife hiding cloth rags and choosing between family needs and buying pads; few women in rural India used pads.
- Lacking volunteers, he tested his own prototypes, wearing a bladder of blood, and faced ridicule and social isolation.
- Big factory machines cost a fortune, so he built a small machine a village group could run.
- He sells to women's self-help groups, not corporations, so the work creates rural jobs as well as health gains.
- He chose impact over wealth, focusing on spreading machines rather than building a big brand.

**Remember:** Transcript not available, so paraphrased: start with one real person's problem, and solve it cheaply enough that others can own the solution.

**Use it at work:**
- Push teams to talk to real users and test rough prototypes on themselves before scaling.
- When a costly platform blocks a problem, ask what the frugal version would look like.
